documents: Kelty & Onderdonk (2022), Episodic deformation and topographic development along the Santa Ynez River fault, Tectonics 41, e2022TC007320 (published PDF, 27 pages)
pages_convention: printed journal pages (printed 'n of 27', identical to PDF pages counted from 1)

entry.evidence: little is known about the late Quaternary deformation style and slip history because the fault is not exposed at the surface

steps.action: Pose the question of how the locus and rate of deformation alternate in the WTR fold and thrust belt over tens of kyr, using the blind Santa Ynez River fault, whose late Quaternary slip history is unknown.
steps.quote: to evaluate how the locus and rates of deformation may alternate in an evolving fold and thrust belt over tens of thousands of years

steps.action: Cite the southward-propagation model of the fold and thrust belt (Levy et al. 2019; Rockwell et al. 1984), and the strain-switching inferences of Niemi & Clark (2018) and Townsend et al. (2018), as untested rivals for the interior of the range.
steps.quote: This model is largely based on observations of late Quaternary faulting along the southern front of the [...]

steps.action: Map seven fluvial and four marine terrace levels remotely from aerial photos, satellite imagery and a 3-m IfSAR DEM, focusing on laterally continuous levels.
steps.quote: We first used historic aerial photos, Google Earth Pro satellite imagery, and a 3-m Digital Elevation Model (DEM)

steps.action: Check and revise the remote mapping in the field, using deposit composition, thickness, weathering and surface morphology to catch DEM misclassifications such as landslides and vineyards.
steps.quote: Our remote mapping was then checked and revised in the field.

steps.action: Survey terrace treads along the valley with a Trimble GeoXH GPS, supplemented by DEM and 1-m LiDAR profiles, and estimate buried marine shoreline-angle elevations by trigonometric projection assuming a 2.29° platform slope.
steps.quote: We performed most of the elevation surveys in the field with a Trimble GeoXH GPS

steps.action: Date four fluvial and two marine terraces by postIR-IRSL on fine-grain feldspar (two samples per site, Central Age Model, gamma-spectrometry dose rates), and Ft1 and Ft3 by AMS radiocarbon on detrital charcoal.
steps.quote: we used post infra-red, infra-red stimulated luminescence (postIR-IRSL) techniques on fine-grain feldspars to measure the depositional age of the terrace sediments

steps.action: Compare paired samples (1-sigma ranges overlap but ages are inverted at most sites), then test partial bleaching by removing tailed aliquots, compare K/U/Th and dose rates with other local studies, and bound water content at 2–20%.
steps.quote: removing the inferred partially bleached aliquots does not change the ages significantly or resolve the age inversions

steps.action: Treat the inversions as measurement error and combine paired ages, and for Ft3 the younger IRSL age with the radiocarbon age, into Bayesian 'preferred' terrace ages.
steps.quote: we regard these apparently inverted sample ages as a result of measurement error

steps.action: Correlate hanging-wall and footwall terraces using profiles and ages, including Ft7 with Mt4 and the Orcutt Formation through cited dates from McGregor & Onderdonk (2021).
steps.quote: All but one of the terraces in the elevated hanging wall of the fault can be correlated with terraces in the footwall.

steps.action: Reject the older footwall Ft5 sample (LSYR-8, 92 ka) as reworked Mt4 material and assign Ft5 a true age of about 65–70 ka, based on elevation and correlation with the 55–75 ka terraces upstream.
steps.quote: There is no clear reason why one sample we measured from this location is older than expected.

steps.action: Compare marine shoreline-angle elevations with highstands on the Simms et al. (2016) GIA-adjusted sea-level curve, prefer a constant coastal uplift of ~1.5 mm/yr over 1.7 mm/yr, and assign Mt3 and Mt2 to ~60 and ~49 ka.
steps.quote: it is more likely that the coast has been uplifting at a relatively constant rate of approximately 1.5 mm/yr

steps.action: Check the premise that incision equals rock uplift: the channel profile is concave, has no knickpoints and is graded to sea level, terrace profiles parallel the channel, and the bedrock is weak.
steps.quote: the channel profile for the lower Santa Ynez River is concave up, devoid of any convexities or knickpoints, and graded to sea level

steps.action: Compute average rock uplift rates with propagated Gaussian uncertainties: 1.8, 1.1 and 0.5 mm/yr for Ft7, Ft5 and Ft3 in the hanging wall, and 1.2 mm/yr for Ft1.
steps.quote: In the hanging wall of the fault, we see a decrease in the average rate of rock uplift through time.

steps.action: Recompute the Ft1 rate assuming the ~15 ka age of Levish et al. (1996) (giving ~0.5 mm/yr) and down-weight the Ft1 rate.
steps.quote: If we assume that the 15 ka is the true age of Ft1, then the corresponding rock uplift rate is approximately 0.5 mm/yr

steps.action: Compute incremental hanging-wall uplift rates (3.2, 2.6 and 0.3 mm/yr) and a nearly constant footwall rate (~1.5 mm/yr) from the marine terraces.
steps.quote: These rates indicate the growth of the Santa Rita hills in the hanging wall of the Santa Ynez River fault was relatively rapid and unsteady

steps.action: Compare deformation of successive terrace levels across the fault: deformation decreases with age, and Ft2 (~32 ka, cited) and Ft1 (6.6 ka) are undeformed.
steps.quote: the lowest two fluvial terraces (Ft1 and Ft2) show no detectable evidence of folding or vertical displacement across the Santa Ynez River fault

steps.action: Keep the reconstruction that the fault was active from ~85 to ~35 ka and inactive since, with regional background uplift affecting both blocks.
steps.quote: we infer that the Santa Ynez River fault has not been active since approximately 35 ka

steps.action: Exclude plate-boundary changes and earthquake-recurrence clustering as causes, on the grounds of the ~50 kyr timescale.
steps.quote: too short a time period to be attributed to large-scale changes in plate boundary tectonics

steps.action: Hypothesize that the episodicity reflects changes in how shortening across the fold and thrust belt is accommodated through time.
steps.quote: this episodic deformation is related to changes in how contractional deformation across the WTR fold and thrust belt is accommodated through time

steps.action: Compare with cited uplift histories of other Santa Maria Basin faults (Purisima and Casmalia hills, Baseline fault), which show synchronous onset and possible decline.
steps.quote: [...] present-day topography in the Santa Rita hills developed in a similar fashion and at the same time as the Purisima and Casmalia hills

steps.action: Reject a direct kinematic link to the Santa Ynez fault, whose cited dip-slip rates did not decrease over 100 kyr.
steps.quote: we infer that it is not directly linked to the Santa Ynez River fault, at least during the past 100 kyr

steps.action: Compare with cited marine-terrace uplift rates along the Santa Barbara–Point Conception coast, which increase as Santa Maria Basin rates decrease, and propose an inverse relationship.
steps.quote: we propose an inverse relationship of timing and deformation rate between faults in the western Santa Barbara Channel and faults in the Santa Maria Basin

steps.action: Reject the progressive southward-propagation model for the western WTR because faults there turn on and off synchronously.
steps.quote: This progressive deformation style does not match the deformation history observed to the west in the Santa Maria Basin

steps.action: Refine the hypothesis into a structural model: modify the Namson & Davis cross section (Figure 12) so the Santa Ynez River fault is a backthrust off the regional detachment, letting strain alternate between structures.
steps.quote: We infer that the linkage of back thrusts in the Santa Maria Basin to this regional detachment creates pathways for strain to be partitioned

steps.action: Exclude surface-process mass redistribution (Simpson 2006) and lateral growth or linkage of thrusts (Bergen et al. 2017) as causes.
steps.quote: we infer that this external force is not a significant factor for the fault slip variability we observed in the WTR fold and thrust belt

steps.action: Conclude that the episodic slip likely reflects shifting transfer of slip from the deep detachment to shallow structures.
steps.quote: episodic slip along the Santa Ynez River fault is likely due to spatial and temporal changes where slip on this deeper detachment is transferred

No; the fault is blind, so it is read from deformed terraces
Timing and rates of fault deformation and uplift
Yes: plate-boundary change, earthquake clustering, surface loading, fault linkage, southward propagation, strain switching
Only qualitatively, through timescale and structural arguments
Found: past terrace surfaces and deposits

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Multiple terrace levels; a prior Plio-Pleistocene episode is inferred
Paired samples, radiocarbon cross-check, bleaching and dose tests, alternative ages and rates
Kept: active ~85–35 ka, inactive since ~35 ka
No review file supplied; reviewers are only acknowledged

end.claim: The blind Santa Ynez River fault deformed terraces in an episode from about 85 to 35 ka, preceded and followed by quiescence, with no slip since ~35 ka; the episodicity is attributed to strain switching between shallow structures above a regional detachment.

decisive_move.sentence: The first postIR-IRSL and radiocarbon dates on the terraces turn deformed and undeformed terrace levels into a timed episode of fault activity.

gates.evidence: The data acquisition (mapping, surveys, dating) was driven by an open problem, the unknown slip history (p. 2), not by a stated hypothesis. The cessation claim could have failed had the dated Ft1/Ft2 terraces been deformed (p. 20). The mechanism hypothesis was stated only after the data (p. 20) and is supported by synthesis, not a test. Nothing was reported as fixed in advance; the preferred-age rules (Table 1 notes) were applied after the inversions were seen.

imports.item: Bayes' theorem combination of Gaussian age distributions into preferred ages
Gamma spectrometry for K, U, Th dose-rate determination
postIR-IRSL protocol and Central Age Model (Buylaert et al. 2009; Galbraith et al. 1999)

novelty_claims.quote: In this paper, we present the first dates for these terraces
Our new mapping and geochronologic data along the Santa Ynez River fault yielded unexpected results
This type of fault activity is unusual

limits: Only the published paper was supplied; reviewers are acknowledged (p. 24) but no review record exists, so no review sequence is coded. Sub-claims at other statuses: the hanging-wall average and incremental uplift rates and the ~1.5 mm/yr footwall rate are estimate_with_resolution (Table 3). The strain-switching mechanism is a hypothesis supported only by synthesis of cited data and qualitative timescale arguments, with no distinct predictions tested (inference). The inverse relationship with the Santa Barbara Channel rests entirely on cited studies. Some gaps limit the record: Ft6 is undated (land access); folding of Ft4/Ft3 is uncertain; the Ft1 age rests on a single charcoal sample; the Ft2 age is cited from Onderdonk et al. 2022; and the Mt3/Mt2 ages come from a sea-level curve, not from dating. Age inversions are resolved by assumption (measurement error), and one footwall sample is set aside ad hoc. The paper does not report how survey lines or sample sites were chosen relative to the expected deformation pattern; that this was done after mapping is inference. The 'unexpected' river migration into the hanging wall (p. 17) is noted but not coded as a separate step.

disagreements.target: Southward propagation of the deformation front (Rockwell et al., 1984; Levy et al., 2019)
disagreements.support: Santa Maria Basin faults, including the Santa Ynez River fault, turned on after ~85 ka and declined synchronously rather than propagating southward.
disagreements.quote: This progressive deformation style does not match the deformation history observed to the west in the Santa Maria Basin

disagreements.target: Drastic westward decrease in late Quaternary deformation rates across the WTR (Levy et al., 2019; Rockwell et al., 1992)
disagreements.support: Measured uplift rates of up to 3.2 mm/yr in the western WTR are comparable to those of the Ventura Basin.
disagreements.quote: This conflicts with previous interpretations of a drastic westward decrease in late Quaternary deformation rates across the WTR

disagreements.target: Santa Ynez River fault as primary splay of, and kinematically linked to, the Santa Ynez fault (Sylvester & Darrow, 1979)
disagreements.support: Cited Santa Ynez fault dip-slip rates were constant or increasing over 100 kyr, while the Santa Ynez River fault stopped at ~35 ka.
disagreements.quote: we infer that it is not directly linked to the Santa Ynez River fault, at least during the past 100 kyr

disagreements.target: ~15 ka age for a strath terrace at Ft1 height (Levish et al., 1996)
disagreements.support: Their radiocarbon data and sample location are unpublished; the new charcoal date gives 6.6 ka.
disagreements.quote: the numeric age reported by Levish et al. (1996) must be considered with caution

disagreements.target: Surface-process mass redistribution as a driver of fault slip variability (Simpson, 2006)
disagreements.support: The authors argue the process matters on timescales over 10^6 years with more extreme climates.
disagreements.quote: we infer that this external force is not a significant factor for the fault slip variability we observed in the WTR fold and thrust belt

disagreements.target: Lateral growth and along-strike linkage of thrusts producing apparent episodic slip (Bergen et al., 2017)
disagreements.support: The WTR structures are long reactivated Miocene normal faults, so growth by linkage is not a viable explanation here.
disagreements.quote: we do not view it as a viable explanation for the Santa Ynez River fault and other major faults within the WTR

disagreements.target: Rivers diverge from rising areas (Holbrook & Schumm, 1999; Ouchi, 1985)
disagreements.support: Mapping shows the antecedent Santa Ynez River migrated into, and was trapped in, the rising hanging wall.
disagreements.quote: This response is surprising because rivers tend to diverge from rising areas and converge in subsiding areas

alternatives_considered.reason: Quartz has poor luminescence characteristics in young orogens; traditional IRSL underestimates ages because of anomalous fading

alternatives_considered.reason: True stratigraphic inversion is not possible, so the inversions are treated as measurement error

alternatives_considered.reason: Elevation ~75 m below Ft7–Mt4 would imply rates of tens of mm/yr; preservation and height mimic the 55–75 ka terraces upstream
